fields.Front:
You lead operations at a regional insurance office and are showing a skeptical colleague where Claude adds value beyond a search engine. You list four requests your team made this week.

Which request benefits most from Claude as a thinking partner rather than a search-style lookup?

A. Look up today's exchange rate from US dollars to euros and tell me which source published the figure.
B. Count the working days that fall between March 3 and March 24, leaving out any public holidays.
C. Read this pasted customer complaint thread and help me work out what the customer wants before I reply.
D. Define a purchase order and an invoice, and tell me which of the two documents is normally issued first.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C requires Claude to reason over material you bring — the complaint thread — and to refine its read through back-and-forth, which is the thinking-partner work Claude adds beyond lookup: the answer needs your situation in it, not a public fact. Option A is a single live fact from one authoritative source, a search box's home ground. Option B is a one-line calculation with nothing of yours in it. Option D is a generic definition that reads the same for everyone; it only becomes thinking-partner work once your specific situation, such as an invoice that arrived without a purchase order, enters the question. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) References: • What are some things I can use Claude for? (Claude Help Center) • When should I use web search, extended thinking, and research? (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front:
A financial analyst on your team wants to upload a 300-page annual report plus its two appendices into a single conversation and ask Claude questions that draw on all of it. She is surprised this is even possible.

Which capability makes this possible?

A. Claude's memory feature saves the full text of uploaded documents and recalls it in later conversations.
B. Claude's context window holds the full text of the report and both appendices while it answers her questions.
C. Claude condenses the whole report into a short summary first and answers her questions from that summary.
D. Claude finds a published copy of the report on the web and answers from that copy rather than from her upload.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: Claude's large context window can ingest 200K+ tokens — about 500 pages of text or more, the figure the Help Center gives for chats on paid plans — so extensive materials can be considered together within one conversation. Option A confuses the context window with memory; uploads inform the current conversation rather than being permanently memorized across all chats. Option C is not how uploads work — Claude parses the file's content rather than replacing it with a lossy summary. Option D is unnecessary and unreliable; the analyst already supplied the document, and the answers should come from the uploaded text, not a web copy. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) References: • How large is the context window on paid Claude plans? (Claude Help Center) • Upload files to Claude: file limits (Claude Help Center) • Context windows (Claude API docs)

fields.Front:
A product manager is weighing three roadmap options with competing tradeoffs. All the relevant data is already pasted into the chat, the decision is genuinely complex, and she cares far more about the quality of the reasoning than about response speed.

Which Claude capability best fits this request?

A. Web search, so Claude gathers additional outside information before it weighs in.
B. A shorter, simpler prompt, so Claude can respond faster and keep the meeting moving.
C. Learning mode, so Claude asks her guiding questions instead of committing to a recommendation.
D. Thinking, so Claude works through the tradeoffs step by step before it answers.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D matches the situation: Thinking lets Claude take time to reason carefully before answering, which suits complex analysis where all the needed information is already in the conversation and quality matters more than speed. Option A adds outside information the problem does not need — the inputs are already pasted in. Option B optimizes for speed, the opposite of the stated priority, and stripping detail from the prompt would weaken the analysis. Option C redirects Claude toward coaching her reasoning rather than delivering the careful analysis she asked for; Learning mode withholds answers by design. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) References: • Change the model, effort, and thinking settings: Use thinking (Claude Help Center) • When should I use web search, extended thinking, and research? (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front:
An HR lead splits her week between an office desktop, a home laptop, and her phone during site visits. She hesitates to start a long-running conversation with Claude because she assumes the work will be stranded on whichever device she used first.

What should she know about working across devices?

A. When signed in, her conversations, projects, memory, and preferences sync across the web, desktop, and mobile apps.
B. Even when signed in, her conversations, projects, and memory stay on the device where they began unless she exports them.
C. When signed in, her conversations sync between the web and desktop apps, but the mobile app keeps its own history.
D. Each of her devices needs its own Claude account, and conversations started on one do not appear on her other devices.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: Claude is available across web, desktop, and mobile apps, and conversations, projects, memory, and preferences sync across devices when you are signed in. Option B invents a manual export step the product does not require. Option C is false — the mobile app syncs with the web and desktop apps like any other device, so nothing starts over on the phone. Option D describes an account model that does not exist and would defeat the purpose of syncing. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) References: • Download Claude: frequently asked questions (claude.com) • What interfaces can I use to access Claude? (Claude Help Center) • Use Claude for Education at your university: access on different devices (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front:
A university instructor wants the 28 students in her seminar to use Claude, which the university provides through Claude for Education, while they prepare for a debate. She worries they will simply collect ready-made conclusions instead of building their own arguments.

Which approach best matches the instructor's goal?

A. Have each student keep the debate readings in a project, so Claude's answers draw on the assigned material.
B. Have students ask Claude to attach a confidence score to each claim, so they know which ones to double-check.
C. Have students ask Claude for the strongest arguments on both sides, so they see the full range before choosing.
D. Have students use Learning mode, so Claude guides their reasoning process rather than providing answers.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is the fit: Learning mode is a Claude experience designed to guide the user's reasoning process rather than hand over answers, which is exactly the critical-thinking outcome the instructor wants. Option A improves the sourcing, since a project's knowledge is loaded into the chats inside it, but well-grounded answers are still answers that students can collect. Option B addresses verification rather than whether students do their own thinking, and self-reported confidence is not a reliable signal anyway. Option C hands students exactly what the instructor fears, ready-made arguments, only for both sides at once. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) References: • Introducing Claude for Education: Learning mode (Anthropic) • Claude for Education (claude.com)

fields.Front:
A marketing manager prompts Claude with 'Write an email about the project delay' and gets a generic message that could apply to any company. The real situation: an enterprise client is facing a second two-week delay to a software integration and has been patient so far.

What change to the prompt will most improve the result?

A. Add the specifics — an enterprise client, a second delay, two weeks, and a professional but apologetic tone.
B. Resubmit the identical prompt several times and keep whichever of the drafts reads least generically.
C. Reply 'make it more professional' and repeat that instruction until the output finally improves.
D. Move the request into a brand-new chat, since a fresh conversation tends to produce far less generic writing.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A targets the root cause: a generic response almost always means the prompt lacked context about the audience, situation, and constraints, and supplying those details is the fix Anthropic's prompting guidance prescribes. Option B is a lottery — regenerating without new information reproduces the same underspecified request. Option C adds a vague adjective rather than the concrete facts Claude is missing. Option D changes the venue, not the information; a new chat with the same thin prompt yields the same thin email. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.1 References: • Prompting best practices: Be clear and direct (Claude API docs) • My prompt isn't giving me a helpful answer (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front:
An HR lead asks Claude for weekly hiring updates and always wants the same layout: a bold header per open role, then three short bullets. Despite asking twice for 'a clean, scannable format,' Claude keeps returning flowing paragraphs.

What is the most effective fix?

A. Ask for each weekly update in far fewer words, so Claude has less room left to write flowing paragraphs.
B. Move the request to a new conversation, so Claude's default formatting habits start from a clean slate.
C. Paste a past update laid out the desired way or spell out the structure, so Claude sees the exact layout she wants.
D. Ask Claude to double-check its formatting against her request, so it catches drift before each weekly update goes out.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C applies the standard rule for format problems: show, don't just tell. Claude understood what to write but not how to present it, and an example or an explicit structure ('a bold header per role, three bullets each') closes that gap. Option A constrains length, not layout — short prose is still prose. Option B does nothing, because the issue is the instruction rather than conversation state. Option D asks Claude to verify against a standard it still has not been given. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.1 References: • Prompting best practices: Use examples effectively (Claude API docs) • Prompting best practices: Control the format of responses (Claude API docs)

fields.Front:
A financial analyst asked Claude about a niche regulatory reporting rule and later discovered that one confident-sounding detail in the response was wrong. She still wants to use Claude for this work, which feeds a report her director signs.

Which TWO practices should she adopt for this kind of high-stakes factual work? (Select TWO.)

A. Independently verify the key facts before any of them go into the director's report.
B. Use web search and ask Claude to cite sources, so responses are grounded in checkable current information.
C. Stop using Claude for anything factual and reserve it strictly for wording, tone, and formatting help.
D. Judge reliability by tone — flag only the answers that sound hedged or uncertain for review.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A and B. Options A and B match Anthropic's guidance for exactly this failure: Claude can occasionally generate plausible but incorrect information, especially on specific facts or niche topics, so ground responses with web search and citations, and verify key facts independently for high-stakes work. Option D is backwards — a confident tone is not a reliability signal, which is precisely why the wrong detail slipped through unnoticed. Option C overcorrects, discarding the research-and-analysis value Claude provides when it is paired with verification. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.1 References: • Claude is providing incorrect or misleading responses. What's going on? (Claude Help Center) • Enable and use web search: How web search works (Claude Help Center) • Reduce hallucinations (Claude API docs)

fields.Front:
A product manager has spent 12 turns trying to steer a draft one-pager. Along the way the conversation absorbed two abandoned outlines and several conflicting instructions, and each new response now mixes pieces of all of them.

What is the fastest way to get back on track?

A. Keep correcting within the same thread, since more accumulated context steadily improves each new output.
B. Ask Claude to disregard everything so far, and then repeat the original prompt to it word for word.
C. Start a new chat with one clearer prompt that consolidates the requirements the failed turns revealed.
D. Turn on the Research feature so that Claude gathers outside examples of well-structured one-pagers.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C reflects sound iteration practice: when a conversation has gone off track, it is often faster to open a new chat with a clearer prompt than to keep redirecting — and the failed turns have revealed exactly what the requirements are. Option A misreads context accumulation; the contradictory instructions in the history are the problem, not the cure. Option B keeps the tangled history in place and re-runs the same underspecified prompt that started the drift. Option D solves a different problem — no outside information is missing here. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.1 References: • Best practices for Claude Code: Course-correct early and often (Claude Code docs) • Context windows: How the context window works (Claude API docs) • Prompting best practices: Be clear and direct (Claude API docs)

fields.Front:
A teacher prompts: 'Write a 250-word newsletter section in a warm, upbeat tone, formatted with a headline and two short paragraphs.' The output is polished but generic — it never lands with its real audience, parents of third-graders anxious about state-testing week.

Which element of an effective prompt is missing?

A. Defining the task — the prompt never actually says what Claude should produce.
B. Specifying rules — the prompt gives Claude no guidance on style, length, or format.
C. Iterating — the request should have been split across several shorter messages.
D. Setting the stage — the prompt omits the writer's role, the audience, and the objective.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D identifies the gap: the prompt defines the task (write a newsletter section) and specifies rules (length, tone, format) but never sets the stage — who is writing, who the parents are, and what the piece must accomplish during testing week — which is why the output is generic. Option A is wrong because the task is clearly stated. Option B is wrong because tone, length, and structure are all specified. Option C names a working habit rather than a part of the prompt, and splitting an underspecified request into pieces would not supply the missing context. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.1 References: • Prompting best practices: Be clear and direct (Claude API docs) • Prompting best practices: Give Claude a role (Claude API docs) • Introduction to prompt design (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front:
A finance team wants to hand Claude a recurring task: drafting the monthly variance commentary that accompanies their reporting package. Before relying on it, the team lead wants evidence that Claude performs well on this specific task.

What is the most practical way to find out?

A. Run a lightweight eval by giving Claude the inputs from 5-10 past commentaries and comparing its drafts to the originals.
B. Ask Claude to rate its own competence at writing variance commentary on a 1-10 scale and proceed once it gives itself a high score.
C. Adopt it for one live reporting cycle and treat the director's reaction to that month's package as the deciding test.
D. Poll other departments for anecdotes about how well Claude handled their documents and extrapolate from those to this task.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is a lightweight eval: collect real examples of the task, create test prompts with the context you would naturally have, compare Claude's outputs against your originals, and refine from what you learn — building evidence before the task matters. Option B relies on self-assessment, which is not a meaningful performance signal. Option C runs the experiment in production, exposing a director-facing deliverable to unvetted output. Option D substitutes other teams' unrelated tasks for evidence about this one; performance is task-specific, which is why evals exist. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.1 References: • Define success criteria and build evaluations: Eval design principles (Claude API docs) • Define success criteria and build evaluations: Define your success criteria (Claude API docs)

fields.Front:
An account manager starts 4-5 Claude chats each week for one client and begins every chat the same way: uploading the client's brand guidelines, two past deliverables, and a tone summary, then re-explaining the account context. She estimates this setup costs her 30 minutes a week.

What is the best way to eliminate this repeated setup?

A. Keep one long-running chat for the client and return to it each week, with the files uploaded once at the start.
B. Create a client project that holds the documents in its knowledge base and the tone and context in its instructions.
C. Create a custom skill that stores the client's past deliverables and account history for Claude to apply in her chats.
D. Ask Claude to memorize the three documents and the account background so it draws on them in future conversations.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is what projects are for: a self-contained workspace whose knowledge base makes the uploaded files available to every chat inside it and whose instructions apply the account context and tone automatically — no re-uploading. Option A crams unrelated threads into one conversation that grows unwieldy and eventually drifts. Option C misuses skills, which encode repeatable procedures rather than storing a client's reference documents and history; that material is knowledge, and it belongs in a project. Option D overstates memory, which retains key context such as your role and preferences, not full reference documents to draw on. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) References: • What are projects? Project knowledge (Claude Help Center) • How can I create and manage projects? Add content to project knowledge (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front:
Your HR team of six shares a project for drafting job descriptions, with templates and past postings already in its knowledge base. Output quality still varies because each member pastes different guidance about tone and structure into their own chats.

How do you make Claude's behavior consistent for everyone in the project?

A. Publish a canonical prompt on the team wiki and ask each member to paste it at the start of every chat.
B. Upload a 'tone guide' document to the knowledge base and rely on Claude to apply it in every conversation.
C. Have each member set personal preferences in their own settings describing the team's desired tone.
D. Write the tone, structure, and template requirements into the project instructions so they apply to every chat.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D uses the mechanism built for this: project instructions guide Claude's behavior across all conversations in the project, so every member gets the same tone and structure without per-chat effort. Option A still depends on six people pasting correctly every time — the inconsistency the team already has. Option B puts behavioral rules in the knowledge base, which supplies background material for Claude to draw on (and, in a large project, is retrieved only when relevant) rather than telling it how to behave in every chat. Option C is per-individual and applies to each member's conversations everywhere, so it neither standardizes the team nor scopes to this project. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) References: • How can I create and manage projects? Add project instructions (Claude Help Center) • Understanding Claude's personalization features: Project instructions (Claude Help Center) • What are projects? Project knowledge (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front:
A research-support project on your company's Team plan has grown to 180 uploaded documents, and the team now sees an indicator that the knowledge base is large. A teammate warns that they must delete files or split the project before Claude 'stops seeing' their material.

What actually happens as project knowledge approaches the context limit?

A. Claude switches to retrieving only the content relevant to each question, which expands capacity by up to 10x.
B. The project stops accepting new uploads until enough older files are removed to bring it back under the limit.
C. Claude silently narrows its attention to the ten most recently uploaded files and ignores everything older.
D. Every chat must begin with the team manually selecting which files should load into context for that session.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A describes the designed behavior on a paid plan: when project knowledge approaches the context window limit, Claude stops loading everything at once and instead searches the project's files, retrieving only what is relevant to the question (Retrieval Augmented Generation), which expands capacity by up to 10x with no setup. Option B describes the hard ceiling projects had before retrieval; on this plan the team can keep adding content. Option C describes a silent recency cutoff the product does not use — retrieval is by relevance, not upload date. Option D adds a manual selection step that retrieval specifically makes unnecessary. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) References: • Retrieval augmented generation (RAG) for projects: How RAG works (Claude Help Center) • What are projects? Enhanced project knowledge with RAG (Claude Help Center) • Glossary: RAG (Claude API docs)

fields.Front: A 60-file client project on an agency's Team plan keeps retrieving the wrong background document when the team asks strategy questions, although the right one is in the knowledge base. Most files carry names like final.pdf, report_v2.pdf, and notes(3).docx. What is the most effective first fix? A. Re-upload the important file at the start of each chat so that it takes precedence over the other project files. B. Split the project into a dozen smaller projects, one per document type, to shrink the space that Claude has to search. C. Rename the files descriptively and name the document when asking, so Claude matches each question to the right file. D. Paste the full text of the key documents into the project instructions so they are loaded at the start of each chat.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C addresses the root cause: Claude uses file names to understand and retrieve the right information, so descriptive names — plus referencing a document by name in the question — directly improve retrieval at almost no effort. Option A works around one file once while leaving the underlying ambiguity in place for the rest of the team's questions. Option B is over-engineered restructuring before the low-effort fix has been tried, and it sacrifices cross-document synthesis. Option D abuses instructions as storage; instructions are for behavioral guidance, and stuffing documents into them bloats every conversation instead of letting retrieval find what is relevant. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) References: • Retrieval augmented generation (RAG) for projects: Best practices for RAG projects (Claude Help Center) • What are projects? Enhanced project knowledge with RAG (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front:
On a Team plan, a marketing lead is sharing a campaign project with eight colleagues. They should be able to open the project, chat with its knowledge, and read everything — but must not change the instructions or swap out knowledge files.

Which permission level should she grant?

A. Owner, so colleagues feel full confidence that the project belongs to the team as much as to her.
B. Can view, which lets members see contents, use the knowledge, and chat, without making any changes.
C. Can edit, since chatting inside a shared project requires edit rights on the workspace.
D. Can comment, a level that lets members chat and leave notes on the project but hides its knowledge files from them.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B matches the requirement exactly: 'Can view' is read-only access with discussion rights — members can see project contents, access the knowledge, and chat, but cannot modify instructions or knowledge. Option A would hand over control of the project itself, far beyond the read-and-chat access the requirement describes. Option C rests on a misconception — chatting does not require edit rights, and granting them would let anyone alter the instructions. Option D describes a permission level that does not exist, and hiding the knowledge files would defeat the purpose of chatting inside the project. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) References: • How can I create and manage projects? To share a project (Claude Help Center) • What are projects? Collaboration and sharing (Claude Help Center) • Manage project visibility and sharing (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front:
An operations manager is auditing how her 12-person team uses Claude and wants to know which of the team's workflows justify creating a dedicated project rather than staying in ordinary one-off chats.

Which TWO workflows are the strongest candidates for a project? (Select TWO.)

A. Monthly board-report drafting that always references the same ten background documents.
B. A one-time request to reformat a single document into a different page layout.
C. Client-email replies from four teammates that must always follow the same tone rules and template.
D. An occasional quick check of a public fact, such as a currency conversion before a wire transfer.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A and C. Options A and C meet the usual criteria for a project: A involves reference materials used repeatedly across chats (the same ten documents every month), and C involves consistent response requirements plus several people who benefit from shared instructions and context. Option B is a one-off task with no recurring knowledge or standing requirements — a plain chat handles it. Option D is a quick lookup that needs neither persistent knowledge nor instructions, so project overhead adds nothing. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) References: • What are projects? Project knowledge (Claude Help Center) • Understanding Claude's personalization features: Project instructions (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front:
A product manager notices that some of Claude's outputs open in a dedicated window beside the conversation while others appear inline in the chat, and asks what determines the difference. He has not changed any settings between the two kinds of response.

When does Claude create an artifact?

A. When the user's request asks for an artifact by name, while other kinds of responses stay inline in the conversation.
B. When the content is significant, self-contained work to be edited, reused, or referenced, while ordinary replies stay inline.
C. When a response runs past one paragraph of text, whatever its content, while shorter replies stay inline in the chat.
D. When the content is interactive code with real logic and user input, while written documents, diagrams, and images stay inline.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B states the actual criteria: Claude automatically creates an artifact for significant, self-contained content (typically over 15 lines) that stands on its own and that you are likely to edit, iterate on, or reuse. Option A is wrong because creation is automatic — an explicit request is only the fallback when Claude does not create one on its own. Option C sets the bar far too low; ordinary conversational answers stay in the chat regardless of length. Option D is wrong because documents, diagrams, SVG images, and HTML pages are all artifact types, not just code. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) References: • What are artifacts and how do I use them? What is an artifact? (Claude Help Center) • What are artifacts and how do I use them? Work with artifacts (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front: A financial analyst asks Claude for two deliverables in one afternoon: a markdown project plan, which appears as an artifact she can watch update in a side window, and an Excel budget workbook, which arrives as a downloadable .xlsx file with no artifact window at all. She asks whether something went wrong. What explains the difference? A. The workbook exceeded the artifact size limit, so Claude automatically downgraded it to a plain file download. B. Artifacts are disabled by default for finance-related content until a workspace admin enables them for her. C. Excel output depends on a Microsoft 365 connector, which she has not yet linked to her Claude account. D. The workbook came from Claude's separate file-creation capability, which returns downloads, not artifacts.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is the actual design: artifacts cover content such as documents, code, single-page websites, images, diagrams, and interactive tools that open beside the chat, while an Excel workbook is built by Claude's separate file-creation capability, which writes a real .xlsx file and hands it back as a download. Option A invents a size-based downgrade path. Option B invents a content-category restriction that does not exist. Option C confuses file creation with connectors — no external integration is involved in generating an Excel file. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) References: • Create and edit files with Claude: Supported file types (Claude Help Center) • What are artifacts and how do I use them? What is an artifact? (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front:
A teacher had Claude build an interactive vocabulary-quiz page as an artifact. She has a list of six unrelated improvements: a new color scheme, a timer, larger fonts, shuffled questions, a score screen, and a print view. The last time she sent Claude a long batch of changes in one message, two of them came back missing and a layout problem appeared that she could not trace to any single request.

What is the most effective way to get all six changes made well?

A. Request the changes one at a time, checking the artifact after each so problems are easy to spot and attribute.
B. Paste all six changes into a single message so the artifact is updated in one consistent pass.
C. Start a fresh conversation and re-describe the entire quiz page with all six improvements built in from the start.
D. Download the page and make the six edits herself in a text editor, then re-upload it for Claude to review.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A follows the artifact best practice of iterating incrementally: one change at a time makes it easy to see what worked, catch issues early, and attribute any regression to the change that caused it — the very problem her last batched request produced. Because the six changes are unrelated, nothing is lost by sequencing them. Option B is tempting for speed, but batching six modifications repeats the failure she already experienced: if the result is off, she cannot tell which request caused it. Option C throws away a working artifact and re-rolls everything from scratch, risking the parts that already worked. Option D abandons the collaborative loop and leaves the teacher hand-editing markup that Claude could revise conversationally. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) References: • What are artifacts and how do I use them? Edit and iterate (Claude Help Center) • Best practices for Claude Code: Course-correct early and often (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front:
An HR lead asks Claude for a reusable onboarding-checklist template she plans to edit and share with three regional offices. Artifacts have opened normally in her other chats, but here Claude writes the whole checklist inline in the chat response instead of creating one.

What is the simplest way to get it as an artifact?

A. Reply 'Please create that as an artifact' — an explicit request is all it takes in the same conversation.
B. Ask a workspace admin to enable artifact creation for her account before trying the request again.
C. Accept the inline version — text templates cannot be artifacts, since only code qualifies for the window.
D. Start a new conversation, because Claude's artifact decision is fixed for the rest of the current chat.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is the simple fix: if Claude does not automatically create an artifact when you expect one, just ask — 'create this as an artifact' — and it will move the content into the artifact window. Option B is unnecessary: artifacts already open for her in other chats, so nothing is switched off for her account or organization. Option C is false; text-heavy documents such as templates and plans are a primary artifact type. Option D is unnecessary because the decision is not locked — a one-line follow-up in the same conversation fixes it. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) References: • What are artifacts and how do I use them? What is an artifact? (Claude Help Center) • Artifacts admin guide for Team and Enterprise plans (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front: A sales-operations manager watches Claude turn her meeting notes into a polished 14-slide PowerPoint file and asks how Claude 'knew' the whole procedure for building a proper .pptx deck. She has not uploaded or configured anything herself. What is running behind the scenes? A. A Microsoft 365 connector that must be linked to her account before Claude can produce the file. B. An Anthropic-built document-creation skill that Claude loads automatically when the task calls for it. C. The artifact window, which converts Claude's markdown response into PowerPoint format on download. D. A custom skill that someone in her organization must have created and uploaded beforehand.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: file-creation capabilities for Excel, PowerPoint, Word, and PDF are powered by Anthropic Skills — packaged expertise that Claude invokes automatically when relevant, with no manual selection. Option A confuses skills with connectors; producing a PowerPoint file requires no link to Microsoft services. Option C is wrong because nothing was converted from a markdown response by the artifact window — the .pptx file was built directly by the file-creation capability and returned as a download. Option D is wrong because document creation is an Anthropic-maintained built-in, not something each organization must author. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.2 References: • What are skills? Anthropic skills (Claude Help Center) • Use skills in Claude: Use Anthropic skills (Claude Help Center) • Create and edit files with Claude: Supported file types (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front:
A financial analyst runs the same quarterly variance analysis four times a year: nine steps, in a fixed order, ending in a specific output format her controller expects. She wants Claude to execute the methodology the same way every quarter.

Which approach best encodes this?

A. Create a project and upload a document describing the nine steps to its knowledge base for Claude to consult.
B. Rely on Claude's memory to accumulate the nine steps gradually over several quarters of conversations.
C. Create a custom skill that encodes the nine-step methodology so Claude follows it whenever the task arises.
D. Keep a master prompt in a spreadsheet and paste all nine steps into each new chat at the start of every quarter.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C applies the dividing line between the two features — projects store knowledge, skills perform tasks. A repeatable, ordered methodology is procedural, exactly what a custom skill encodes so Claude executes it consistently every time. Option A treats the process as reference material: project knowledge is static background for the chats inside that one project, not a procedure Claude runs wherever the task comes up. Option B stretches memory beyond its purpose of retaining key context such as role and preferences — it is not a place to encode a formal methodology. Option D works but reintroduces the manual, error-prone repetition that skills exist to remove. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.2 References: • What are skills? Skills vs. projects (Claude Help Center) • Skills overview: Compare skills with other features (Claude docs) • How to create custom skills (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front:
A brand manager with no technical background wants a custom skill that applies her company's brand-voice rules whenever Claude reviews marketing copy. She assumes building it means writing configuration files.

What is the easiest way to create the skill?

A. Only Anthropic can create skills, so she should submit a request through the support channel.
B. Ask her IT department to code the skill's folder structure and upload the finished package for her.
C. Author the skill's instruction files by hand, following the published specification line by line, then upload them.
D. Describe the workflow to Claude in a chat, answer its questions, upload the brand guide, and save the file it generates.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is the low-effort path: the easiest way to create a custom skill is through conversation — Claude interviews you about the workflow, incorporates uploaded reference materials like templates and style guides, and generates the properly structured skill file for you to save; no coding is required. Option A is wrong because custom skills exist precisely so users and organizations can create their own. Options B and C both assume manual technical authoring that conversational creation makes unnecessary — hand-building the structure is the hard path, not the requirement. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.2 References: • Introducing Agent Skills: Getting started (claude.com) • Create custom skills: Decide what skill to create (Claude docs) • How to create custom skills (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front:
An HR lead saved a custom skill that structures meeting notes into her team's format and turned it on in her settings. A colleague asks how the skill will get applied when she opens a new conversation to work on meeting notes.

How do skills get used in practice?

A. Claude loads the skill on its own whenever a request fits what it does, since enabling it makes it available in her chats.
B. Claude loads the skill after she picks it from a menu in each chat, since it does not choose skills on its own.
C. Claude loads the skill inside the project where she created it, since skills belong to a single project.
D. Claude loads the skill after she pastes its instructions into a chat, since it does not keep them between conversations.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is how skills work: Claude handles skill selection automatically based on your request — when a task is relevant, the skill loads, and you will see it mentioned as Claude works. Option B turns an optional step into a requirement: she can pick a skill herself, but nothing has to be selected at the start of a chat. Option C invents a project boundary; skills are enabled for your account, not scoped to one project. Option D defeats the purpose of skills, which is that the packaged instructions apply automatically instead of being re-pasted. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.2 References: • Skills overview: Find, turn on, and use skills (Claude docs) • What are skills? How do skills work? (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front:
An operations manager finds a custom skill file on a public forum that promises to automate her vendor-audit checklist and save three hours a week. The post is anonymous, and she is tempted to install the skill immediately.

What should she do first?

A. Install it and test it on a sample checklist first, since skills are plain-text instructions, not code that runs.
B. Review the skill's contents and check that its source is trustworthy first, since skill files include scripts.
C. Install it into a private project to start with, since a project keeps a skill's effects contained there.
D. Read the forum replies first and install it once several users confirm it works, since a popular skill has been tested.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is the standard security guidance: because skills can include executable code, install custom skills only from trusted sources and review the contents of anything from an external source before use. Option A rests on a false premise — skills are folders of instructions, scripts, and resources, and can include executable code. Option C misunderstands scoping; projects do not sandbox a skill's behavior. Option D puts popularity in place of review: replies from other anonymous users say that the skill runs, not what its scripts do or who wrote it, and custom skills are not individually vetted by Anthropic, so that review responsibility is hers. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.2 References: • Use skills in Claude: What are the primary risks of using skills? (Claude Help Center) • Skills overview: Find, turn on, and use skills (Claude docs) • Introducing Agent Skills: Getting started (claude.com)

fields.Front:
A product manager spends 30-40 minutes a day copying content out of her project tracker and team chat into Claude conversations so it has the context to draft status updates and answer questions.

What is the best way to eliminate this manual shuttling?

A. Create a project and upload weekly CSV exports of both tools to its knowledge base so every chat can reference them.
B. Maintain a running summary document of both tools by hand and paste it into each conversation.
C. Take a screenshot of each tool's dashboard every morning and attach the images to her first chat.
D. Connect the tools so Claude can search and read them directly from within the conversation.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is what connectors are for: they give Claude access to the tools and data you already use, so it can search files, retrieve records, and — depending on the permissions granted — perform actions, all from within the conversation. Option A uses a real feature for the wrong job: a knowledge base holds reference material, and weekly exports leave Claude answering from data that is up to a week stale while still costing her the export step. Option B has her maintaining a second copy of her tools by hand, which is the overhead she is trying to remove. Option C delivers unstructured pixels once a day rather than live, searchable data. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.4 References: • Use connectors to extend Claude's capabilities: What are connectors? (Claude Help Center) • Get started with connectors: Use the connector in a conversation (Claude docs)

fields.Front:
While setting up connectors, an operations director sees that a document store, a chat platform, and a payment service are all offered as connectors in Claude, and asks how one assistant can integrate with so many unrelated products.

What makes this possible?

A. Per-product API integrations, which Anthropic builds and maintains separately for each supported product.
B. Per-tool fine-tuned models, each trained on a single tool's data and shipped inside that tool's connector.
C. The Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard that gives any tool one consistent way to connect to Claude.
D. Screen automation, in which Claude signs in to each tool with her credentials and operates it like a person.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: connectors are powered by MCP, an open standard that works like USB-C for AI — one universal interface, so the developers of any tool can build a connector that works seamlessly with Claude. Option A describes a closed, bespoke model that an open standard specifically replaces, and it could never scale to a whole directory of tools. Option B misunderstands the architecture — the same Claude works across all connected tools. Option D describes credential sharing and interface browsing; connectors are authorized through each tool's own permission grant and exchange data through the protocol rather than by driving the tool's screens. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.4 References: • What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)? (MCP docs) • Introducing the Model Context Protocol (Anthropic) • Use connectors to extend Claude's capabilities: What are connectors? (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front:
A financial analyst wants Claude to work with two kinds of material: contract records in a cloud documentation service that she signs in to, and a folder of about 200 files stored locally on her computer and nowhere else.

How should she set up access?

A. Web connectors for both sources, each set up in the browser at claude.ai, since a web connector reaches local files too.
B. A web connector for the cloud service and a desktop extension in Claude Desktop for the local files, since extensions run locally.
C. A web connector for the cloud service and manual uploads of the local files, since Claude cannot connect to files on her computer.
D. Desktop extensions in Claude Desktop for both sources, since extensions have replaced web connectors for cloud services too.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B reflects the two connector types: web connectors link Claude to cloud services, while desktop extensions run locally through the Claude Desktop app and give Claude access to local files and native applications. Option A cannot cover the local folder — browser-configured web connectors reach cloud services, not her file system. Option C ignores desktop extensions, whose local file access exists precisely to avoid endless manual uploads. Option D gets the relationship wrong: the two types serve different territories and complement rather than replace each other. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.4 References: • When to use desktop and web connectors: Quick guide (Claude Help Center) • Use connectors to extend Claude's capabilities (Claude Help Center) • Desktop Extensions: one-click MCP server installation for Claude Desktop (Anthropic Engineering)

fields.Front:
A marketing team of nine is eager to connect its shared drive and chat workspace to Claude, but their director hesitates, worried that connecting will give Claude — and therefore every team member — unrestricted, permanent access to everything in those systems.

Which TWO facts accurately address the director's concern? (Select TWO.)

A. Claude's access is limited to the data the connecting user already has permission to see in the underlying tool.
B. Connected services are automatically limited to read-only access during an initial trial period after connection.
C. Connectors grant organization-wide visibility, beyond what each connecting user is allowed to see in the connected tools.
D. Access is revocable at any time from Claude's settings or the service's own settings, with permissions adjusted individually.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A and D. Options A and D describe the connector security model: Claude sees what you see — connecting your account exposes only data you already have access to, never someone else's inbox or restricted folders — and access is both scoped and revocable at any time from either side of the connection, with individual permissions that can be toggled. Option B invents a probationary read-only period that does not exist; what a connector can do is governed by the permissions granted, not a timer. Option C is the very misconception being corrected — connectors do not grant visibility beyond each user's existing permissions, so there is nothing to relocate. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.4 References: • Use connectors to extend Claude's capabilities: Security and privacy (Claude Help Center) • Get started with connectors: Manage or disconnect a connector (Claude docs) • Use connectors to extend Claude's capabilities: What are connectors? (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front:
An HR lead finds an unofficial connector for her niche HR system, written by an individual developer and shared on a personal blog. It is not listed in Claude's connector directory, and she wants the two hours a week it promises to save.

What is the right approach before connecting it?

A. Connect it and watch how it behaves, since connectors are read-only by design and a bad one costs little more than time.
B. Confirm that it is built on the Model Context Protocol before connecting it, since the open standard makes compliant connectors safe.
C. Vet the source before connecting it, since a connector acts with the access she grants, including changing her data.
D. Connect it now and revoke its access later if its behavior seems off, since revoking afterwards undoes whatever it did.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is the right posture: only add connectors from sources you trust — a connector operates with the access you grant, which can include reading and modifying data, so the source's trustworthiness is the gating question. Option A rests on a false premise, since connectors can take actions, not just read. Option B checks the wrong thing: the Model Context Protocol is an open standard for how a connector connects to Claude, and following it says nothing about who wrote the connector or what it does with her data; a connector she adds herself has not been reviewed by Anthropic at all, and even a directory listing is not a security audit. Option D is backwards risk management: revoking access after the fact cannot undo what an untrustworthy connector already accessed. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.4 References: • Connector verification: Stay safe with third-party connectors (Claude docs) • Add an unlisted connector: Security and privacy (Claude docs) • Use connectors to extend Claude's capabilities: Custom connectors (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front:
A product manager connected her project-management tool three weeks ago. Claude summarizes her task list flawlessly, but when she asks it to create a new task for the budget review, it reports that it cannot.

What is the most likely explanation and fix?

A. Connectors are read-only by design, so she should create tasks by hand in the tool instead of asking Claude.
B. The connector's permissions cover reading but not creating tasks, so she should review them and allow that action.
C. Creating tasks needs the desktop-extension version of the connector, so she should swap out the web connector.
D. Write access needs its own account, so she should reconnect the tool under a second account reserved for write operations.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B matches how connectors work: what Claude can do in a connected tool depends on the connector and the permissions you grant — reading and taking actions are distinct capabilities, and tool permissions can be set individually for each connector. On Team and Enterprise plans an owner can also block an action for the whole organization, which individual users cannot override. Option A is false as a design claim; connectors can create content, update records, and execute tasks when permitted. Option C confuses the web/desktop split, which is about where tools live (cloud versus local), not read-versus-write capability. Option D adds account juggling that no part of the permission model requires. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.4 References: • Get started with connectors: Manage or disconnect a connector (Claude docs) • Use connectors to extend Claude's capabilities: Restrict actions within connected services (Claude Help Center) • Use connectors to extend Claude's capabilities: Connect a service to Claude (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front:
A new operations coordinator has questions in her first week: how to submit expenses, what was decided in last month's pricing discussions, and who owns the vendor-onboarding process. The answers are scattered across her company's document stores, chat threads, and email.

Which capability is purpose-built for these questions?

A. Enterprise search — the 'Ask your org' project that searches connected company sources and answers with citations.
B. The Research feature, which conducts a deep, multi-angle investigation of the question across the public web.
C. A regular chat in which she pastes as detailed a description of the company as she can assemble on her own.
D. An artifact that renders the employee handbook as an interactive, searchable page she can keep open.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is the designed fit: enterprise search adds a dedicated, preconfigured 'Ask your org' option that searches across connected company tools — documents, chat, email — and synthesizes cited answers, exactly the policy, decision, and who-owns-what questions of onboarding. Option B points the investigation at the public web, where none of these internal answers live. Option C depends on whatever the coordinator can paste, which is precisely what she does not yet know. Option D repackages one document, while her questions span many sources beyond any handbook. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) References: • Use enterprise search: What is enterprise search? (Claude Help Center) • Use enterprise search: How does enterprise search work? (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front:
A finance director learns her company is enabling enterprise search and objects: the company drive, which each employee connects by signing in with their own account, contains payroll folders, and she assumes anything connected becomes searchable by all 400 employees.

How does enterprise search actually handle access?

A. All connected content becomes searchable by all members, so sensitive folders must be disconnected first.
B. Results respect each user's existing permissions in the source tools, and connected data is not indexed separately.
C. Content is copied into a separate Claude-managed index, where the source system's permissions no longer apply to it.
D. Access is controlled by asking employees to avoid searching for sensitive topics such as compensation.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is the security model: enterprise search only shows what the asking user already has permission to access in the original connected tool, conversations remain private, and connected data is not indexed or stored separately. Option A is the misconception being corrected — connection does not flatten permissions. Option C describes a shadow-copy architecture that is the opposite of how the feature works. Option D is policy by request rather than enforcement; a stated norm would not technically prevent access, and it is not how the product controls anything. The one exception the Help Center notes is a custom connector set up with a shared credential, where results reflect what that credential can reach — not the case here, since each employee signs in individually. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) References: • Use enterprise search: Privacy and permissions (Claude Help Center) • Use connectors to extend Claude's capabilities: Security and privacy (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front:
A recruiter at a firm called Meridian hears that enterprise search is now set up, and an 'Ask Meridian' project appears starred in her sidebar. Her first questions return thin results that miss documents and threads she knows exist and can open herself.

What is the most likely reason?

A. The owner's configuration finished the setup, so the thin results are everything search can reach for her.
B. Enterprise search starts from the date it was enabled, so older documents and email threads are missing from the results.
C. The project searches files uploaded to its knowledge base, so she has to upload the missing documents herself.
D. Each user also authenticates her own services after the owner's setup, so search skips the ones she has not connected.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D explains the thin results: enterprise search requires an owner to configure the organization's connectors and then each user to authenticate with the services they want searched; until the recruiter completes her own guided onboarding and connects her accounts, Claude cannot search those sources for her, and she can add more connectors later for broader coverage. Option A misses the second, per-user step entirely. Option B invents a start-date restriction that does not exist. Option C misunderstands the feature — it searches connected tools where content already lives, not a manually maintained upload set. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) References: • Use enterprise search: For users (Claude Help Center) • Use enterprise search: My search results seem incomplete (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front:
A benefits manager must recommend one of three payroll providers to her CFO in two weeks. She needs pricing, implementation timelines, and support quality compared across all three, with sources she can hand to procurement for verification.

Which capability fits this task?

A. A quick web search, since each provider's pricing page is public and easy to find with one or two queries.
B. Thinking, so that Claude reasons carefully through which provider is the best overall choice for her company.
C. Research, which runs a multi-search, multi-source investigation and delivers a synthesized, cited report.
D. A normal chat that asks Claude to recall whatever it already knows about each of the three providers.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C matches every signal in the stem: comparative analysis across multiple criteria, information that must be gathered from many sources, synthesis into one deliverable, and verifiable citations — the profile of a Research task. Option A is sized for a single quick fact from one or two sources, not a three-vendor, three-criteria comparison. Option B is for problems solvable by reasoning alone; this task's bottleneck is gathering current outside information, which Thinking does not do. Option D relies on recall without gathering or citing current sources, exactly the wrong basis for a procurement-facing recommendation. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.6 References: • When should I use web search, extended thinking, and research? Research (Claude Help Center) • Use research on Claude (Claude Help Center) • Claude takes research to new places (claude.com)

fields.Front:
A product manager kicks off her first Research run on a market-sizing question and is surprised to watch progress indicators for several minutes instead of getting the near-instant answer she is used to from a normal chat.

Why does Research take this long?

A. Research queues each request behind other users' investigations, so the wait depends on how busy the service is.
B. Research is agentic and multi-step, so Claude plans, runs searches that build on each other, and then synthesizes.
C. Research reads the public web exhaustively before it starts writing, so the process takes minutes at the least.
D. Research caches results the first time a feature is used, so the first run is slow and later runs are fast.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B describes what the time buys: Research plans its approach with Thinking, conducts multiple searches where each round is informed by what the last one found — sometimes across hundreds of sources — pursues leads and fills gaps autonomously, and then synthesizes everything into a cited report; that work is not instant by nature. Option A attributes the delay to queueing rather than to the investigation itself. Option C overstates the process; Claude searches selectively and iteratively, not exhaustively. Option D invents a caching warm-up that has nothing to do with why a multi-search investigation takes minutes. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.6 References: • Use research on Claude (Claude Help Center) • Claude takes research to new places (claude.com) • How we built our multi-agent research system (Anthropic Engineering)

fields.Front:
A marketing manager used Research to produce a 20-page competitive brief she will present to leadership in three days. Before circulating it, she wants confidence that its factual claims about competitors hold up.

What is the most reliable way to check the report?

A. Ask Claude to append a confidence percentage to each claim and review only the low-scoring ones.
B. Re-run the identical Research prompt and keep only the claims that appear in both reports.
C. Accept the findings as they stand, since Research already cross-references multiple sources.
D. Use the citations attached to the report's claims to spot-check the underlying sources directly.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D uses the feature built for this: a Research report comes with citations that link its claims back to their sources, making verification fast — she can open the citations behind the claims that matter most and confirm them herself. Option A lets self-reported confidence decide what goes unchecked, and a model's stated confidence is not a dependable signal of accuracy. Option B is slow and can simply reproduce the same error twice, providing consistency rather than truth. Option C outsources her accountability; cross-referencing during research reduces errors but does not replace human verification before a leadership presentation. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.6 References: • Use research on Claude (Claude Help Center) • Claude is providing incorrect or misleading responses. What's going on? (Claude Help Center) • Reduce hallucinations (Claude API docs)

fields.Front:
An office manager is about to launch a Research run to plan a 20-person team offsite. Her draft prompt reads, in full: 'Tell me about team offsite options.' A colleague suggests investing another five minutes in the prompt, since the run itself will take a while.

Which TWO changes would most improve the report she gets back? (Select TWO.)

A. Tell Claude to write one clean narrative, leaving out references such as citations, footnotes, and source links.
B. State the specific goal and constraints, such as group size, budget range, dates, and acceptable travel radius.
C. Specify the structure she wants, such as sections for venue options, costs, logistics, and a recommendation.
D. Ask for an exhaustive report, covering topics such as venues, activities, caterers, transport, and lodging.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B and C. Options B and C are the prompt strategies that pay off in Research: be specific about goals and include relevant constraints (budget, timeline, geography) so Claude investigates options that actually fit, and specify the sections you want because Claude organizes its findings around the structure you provide. Option A strips out the citations she needs to verify venues and prices before committing budget, trading verifiability for polish. Option D confuses breadth with usefulness — without goals or constraints, an exhaustive report is just a longer list of options that may not fit her group, budget, or dates. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.6 References: • Prompting best practices: Research and information gathering (Claude API docs) • Prompting best practices: Be clear and direct (Claude API docs) • Use research on Claude (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front:
A program manager wants one briefing that combines what her own team has already discussed about 'Project Atlas' in email and internal documents with current industry best practices from the public web. Her workspace tools are connected to Claude.

How should she approach this?

A. Run Research once, steering it to pull from her connected email and documents and then research web best practices.
B. Research reaches only the public web, so she should paste the internal threads into the prompt beforehand.
C. Run Research for the web half, upload the internal documents to a separate chat, and merge the outputs by hand.
D. Internal sources are reachable only through enterprise search, so a combined briefing is not possible in one run.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A uses Research as designed: with integrations connected, Research pulls context from your emails, calendar, and documents alongside web research in a single investigation, and you can steer it by naming the sources to draw from — for example, 'summarize what has been discussed about Project Atlas across my email and documents, then research industry best practices for similar initiatives.' Option B understates the feature — connected integrations are exactly how Research reaches internal context without pasting. Option C splits one supported workflow into two manual halves and pushes the synthesis onto her. Option D confuses two capabilities; enterprise search is one way to query org knowledge, but Research can also draw on connected integrations while investigating the web. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.6 References: • Use research on Claude: Use research (Claude Help Center) • Claude takes research to new places (claude.com) • Claude can now connect to your world (claude.com)

fields.Front:
Every Monday an operations manager spends about 45 minutes on the same routine: checking messages, pulling numbers from a spreadsheet, assembling a status document, and prepping for the day's meetings. Her messaging tool and shared drive are connected to Claude. The steps never change, and the output is a formatted document her team expects by 9 a.m.

What is the most effective way to work with Claude on this?

A. Run it turn by turn in a chat each Monday morning, asking Claude one question for each step of the routine.
B. Hand it off once as a scheduled task, so Claude runs the sequence on cadence and she reviews the document.
C. Ask Claude to summarize each meeting after it happens instead of preparing the Monday status document at all.
D. Dictate the routine by voice each Monday morning so the same steps take less typing time to work through.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B recognizes the shape of the work: a multi-step sequence, a real deliverable, and a recurring schedule are the signals for handing work off rather than chatting — set it up once as a scheduled task and Claude gathers the inputs, produces the document, and she reviews the result. Option A keeps her stitching the steps together manually every week, which is the 45 minutes she is trying to reclaim. Option C changes the deliverable rather than automating it. Option D changes the input method while leaving the manual, step-by-step Monday routine fully intact. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) References: • Schedule recurring tasks in Claude Cowork: What scheduled tasks can do (Claude Help Center) • Schedule recurring tasks in Claude Cowork: How scheduled tasks work (Claude Help Center) • Claude Cowork and chat are one Claude (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front:
A financial analyst inherited a 12-tab workbook from a departed colleague. She needs the calculation flows explained and several assumptions updated without breaking the formula dependencies — and she wants to stay inside the spreadsheet while doing it.

Which way of working with Claude best fits?

A. Upload the workbook to a claude.ai chat and download a freshly generated copy after each round of changes.
B. Paste screenshots of each tab into a conversation and transcribe the suggested changes back into the file.
C. Use Claude for Excel, whose sidebar explains formula flows and updates inputs in place in the open workbook.
D. Rebuild the model from scratch in a new file so there are no legacy formulas or dependencies to worry about.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C matches both constraints: Claude for Excel brings Claude into the spreadsheet as a sidebar, where it can explain how formulas and calculation flows work across sheets and update inputs while preserving formula relationships — editing in place rather than round-tripping files. Option A works for analysis but produces a new downloaded version each cycle instead of working in the open file, exactly the workflow she wants to avoid. Option B gives Claude flat images of a live model and leaves every edit to manual transcription. Option D discards a working, if opaque, model and is a far bigger project than understanding and extending it. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) References: • Use Claude for Excel: What you can do (Claude docs) • Use Claude for Excel: Understand complex models (Claude docs)

fields.Front:
A marketing manager returns from a week away to find that a campaign decision unfolded across four long Slack threads totaling several hundred messages. Her company has Claude Tag set up in the campaign channel. She needs to catch up and post an informed reply, without leaving Slack or forwarding the content elsewhere.

What is the best way to use Claude here?

A. Copy each thread into a claude.ai conversation, get a summary, and paste her drafted reply back into Slack.
B. Ask IT for a weekly export of channel history so she can review the decision in a separate document.
C. Start a Research run on the campaign topic so Claude can reconstruct what was decided from outside sources.
D. Tag Claude in the threads so it summarizes each discussion and helps her draft a reply without leaving Slack.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is the purpose-built fit: Claude Tag brings Claude into Slack, where tagging it in a thread lets it summarize lengthy discussions, break down what was decided, and help draft responses without leaving the workspace — meeting her stay-in-Slack constraint. Option A reaches the same information the long way, with manual copying that her constraint rules out. Option B introduces delay and an export process for something Claude can read in place. Option C points an investigation at the public web when the needed context is the internal threads themselves. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) References: • What is Claude Tag? (Claude Help Center) • Claude Tag: Catch up, get a one-off recap (Claude docs) • Work with Claude Tag: Common uses (Claude docs)

fields.Front:
Between back-to-back meetings, a product manager working on her Mac is staring at an unfamiliar KPI dashboard in a vendor tool. She needs the metrics explained in the next five minutes, while keeping the dashboard on screen.

What is the fastest way to get Claude's help on her desktop?

A. Use the desktop app's quick entry to pull Claude up over her work and share a screenshot of the dashboard.
B. Retype the dashboard's metric names and current values into a browser chat tab and ask for an explanation.
C. Set up a connector for the vendor tool first so Claude can query the underlying data source directly.
D. Create a scheduled task that analyzes the dashboard every week and reports the trends back to her.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A uses the desktop app's native strengths for exactly this moment: quick entry pulls Claude up over whatever you are working on in a compact window that stays on top, and a screenshot or shared window lets Claude see what you see — no transcription, dashboard still in view. Option B is slow, error-prone manual copying that loses the visual layout. Option C is heavy setup for a five-minute question, and a connector for a niche vendor tool may not even exist. Option D solves a recurring-reporting problem she does not have; the need is immediate and one-time. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) References: • Use quick entry with Claude Desktop on Mac: Key features (Claude Help Center) • Use quick entry with Claude Desktop on Mac: Capture a screenshot (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front: A product manager uses Claude with a custom connector to an MCP server that her company's engineers wrote for its project-management tool; she connected it three weeks ago. In the connector's settings, every tool it exposes is set to Always allow. Claude summarizes her task list flawlessly by calling the connector's list_my_tasks tool. When she asks which tasks mention the budget review, Claude runs its built-in web search and reports that it found nothing relevant, although the connector's search_tasks tool does full-text search across task titles, descriptions and comments. That tool's description reads only "Search." When she tells Claude to call search_tasks by name, it returns the right tasks. What is the most likely explanation and fix? A. The connector's permissions cover listing tasks but not searching them, so she should review its tool permissions and allow the search tool. B. Claude's built-in web search takes precedence over connector tools, so she should tell Claude in each chat about her tasks not to search the web. C. The search tool was added to the server after she first connected, so she should disconnect the connector and reconnect it to reload the list of tools. D. The search tool's description tells Claude too little about when to use it, so the engineers should expand it to say what it searches and returns.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Claude decides which tool fits a request mainly from the tools' descriptions, so a tool described only as "Search." gives it no basis for recognizing that task questions belong there, and it falls back on a built-in tool it understands. The facts rule out an access problem: every tool is set to Always allow, and search_tasks works when named. Option D fixes the cause by having the server's authors describe what the tool searches, what it returns and when to use it. Option A is the remedy for a tool that is blocked or needs approval, which is not the situation here. Option B assumes a fixed priority that the scenario contradicts, since Claude called list_my_tasks with web search available; forbidding web search would leave the search tool no easier to recognize. Option C cannot be right, because a tool missing from the connector's tool list could not be called by name. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.4 References: • Define tools: Best practices for tool definitions (Claude API docs) • Get started with connectors: Manage or disconnect a connector (Claude docs)

fields.Front:
At a logistics company, the platform team is connecting Claude Code to two systems. One is a widely used commercial issue tracker; a maintained community MCP server covers every tracker operation the team needs. The other is a dock-scheduling rules engine that the company wrote itself: its internal API checks a proposed slot against the scheduling rules and explains any rejection, and that logic lives in the engine's code. The engine stores its bookings in PostgreSQL, for which a maintained community MCP server exists; no MCP server exists for the engine itself. The team wants Claude to file tracker issues and to check slots while it works on scheduling code.

Which design should the team choose?

A. Write custom servers for both the tracker and the rules engine, and retire the community tracker server.
B. Adopt the community tracker server, and write a custom server that exposes the rules engine's operations.
C. Adopt the community tracker server, and reach the rules engine through the community PostgreSQL server.
D. Adopt the community tracker server, and fork its code to add the rules engine's operations to the same server.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. The exam guide's rule for MCP integrations is to choose existing community servers for standard integrations and to reserve custom servers for team-specific workflows. The tracker is the standard case: a maintained community server already covers what the team needs. The rules engine is the team-specific case: its check-and-explain logic exists only in the company's own code, so only a server written around its API can offer those operations as tools. That is Option B. Option A rebuilds, and then has to maintain, an integration that already exists. Option C looks like reuse, but a database server exposes the bookings tables, not the rule logic, so Claude would be guessing at rules the engine already implements. Option D leaves the team maintaining a fork of the tracker server and gains nothing, because tools from every configured server are available in the same session. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.4 References: • Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP: Find and build MCP servers (Claude Code docs) • Example Servers: Community implementations (MCP docs) • Build an MCP server (MCP docs)

fields.Front:
A financial analyst uses Claude for many kinds of work: variance analyses, emails to her controller, slide outlines and one-off questions, in several projects and in ordinary chats. Her nine-step quarterly variance methodology is encoded in a custom skill. She wants three conventions followed in all of her work with Claude, whatever the task: amounts in thousands of euros, quarters labeled by fiscal year, and British spelling. The conventions are not steps of any one procedure; they are standards that every response should meet.

Which approach best encodes the three conventions?

A. Write the conventions into her account-wide instructions for Claude, which are applied to all of her conversations.
B. Create a second custom skill that holds the conventions, which Claude loads when a request matches its description.
C. Add the conventions to the instructions of her most-used project, which apply to the chats inside that project.
D. Save the conventions in a note to paste into each new chat, which shows them to Claude from the first message.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. The exam guide separates on-demand, task-specific workflows, which belong in skills, from universal standards, which belong in instructions that are always loaded (in Claude Code, CLAUDE.md, read at the start of every session). The three conventions are standards for every response, not a procedure for one task, so they belong in the always-applied place the Claude apps offer: account-wide instructions, which are applied to all conversations. That is Option A. Option B is right for her variance methodology, but a skill is task-specific and loads only when Claude finds a request relevant to its description, so it is the wrong vehicle for rules that must hold in an email as much as in an analysis. Option C is always applied, but only to chats inside one project, and she also works in other projects and in ordinary chats. Option D depends on her remembering to paste the note every time, which standing instructions make unnecessary. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.2 References: • What are skills?
