Skills vs. custom instructions (Claude Help Center) • Understanding Claude's personalization features: Instructions for Claude (Claude Help Center) • Extend Claude Code: Compare similar features (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front: In its repository's .claude/skills/ directory, a support-tooling team keeps a project skill named handoff-notes. A developer runs it at the end of a long Claude Code session; its instructions tell Claude to write up the decisions made and the dead ends hit during that session so that a colleague can pick the work up. The notes come to about fifteen lines. A reviewer proposes adding context: fork to the skill's frontmatter, arguing that a skill's output should be kept out of the main conversation. How should the team respond to the proposal? A. Accept it, so that the notes are written by a subagent and a short result is what returns to the session. B. Accept it and set agent: Explore, so that a read-only subagent collects the session's decisions. C. Decline it, so that the skill keeps running inline, where the session's conversation history is available. D. Decline it and move the instructions into CLAUDE.md, so that the handoff steps load in every session.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. context: fork runs a skill in an isolated subagent: the skill's content becomes the subagent's prompt, and the subagent does not see the conversation history. That isolation suits skills whose verbose or exploratory output would clutter the session. This skill is the opposite case: its input is the session itself and its output is about fifteen lines, so it should run inline, the default, where it has the conversation context. That is Option C. Option A would hand the task to a subagent with nothing to summarize, so the notes would be empty or invented. Option B has the same gap, because a forked skill that uses the Explore agent sees only the skill's content and that agent's system prompt. Option D confuses two mechanisms: CLAUDE.md holds standing conventions and is loaded in every session, whereas a handoff procedure run at the end of some sessions is an on-demand task, which is what a skill is for. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.2 References: • Extend Claude with skills: Run skills in a subagent (Claude Code docs) • Extend Claude with skills: Types of skill content (Claude Code docs) • Extend Claude Code: Compare similar features (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front: An HR lead has Claude triage about 40 employee questions from a shared inbox each week, tagging each one urgent, this week or routine. The triage arrives in the layout she wants: a bold header per question, then three short bullets. The tags vary from week to week. A payroll underpayment was tagged routine one week and a nearly identical one urgent the week after, and a question about parking permits was tagged urgent. Her prompt's only guidance on tagging is "tag each question by how pressing it is." What is the most effective fix? A. Paste one of the past triages into the prompt as a sample of the output she expects each week. B. Define each tag in the prompt with explicit criteria and one example question that belongs under it. C. Tell Claude to be cautious with the urgent tag and to apply it when it is highly confident. D. Ask Claude to check every tag against her instruction a second time before it returns the weekly triage.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. The layout is already right, so the fault is in classification: "how pressing it is" leaves Claude to redraw the boundary between tags each week. The exam guide's remedy for inconsistent severity labels is explicit criteria for each level together with a concrete example of each, which is Option B: the prompt says what makes a question urgent, this week or routine and shows one question under each. Option A is the fix when the format is wrong; a past triage demonstrates headers and bullets that Claude already produces, and it carries that week's tags, mistaken ones included, without stating where the boundaries lie. Option C sets a general bar of caution and confidence but does not say what belongs under each tag, so a payroll error could land under any of them. Option D asks Claude to verify the tags against the same vague instruction, which gives it no standard to check them against. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.1 References: • Prompting best practices: Use examples effectively (Claude API docs) • Prompting best practices: Be clear and direct (Claude API docs) • Code Review: What you can tune (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front:
Each week a marketing manager has Claude review the 30 or so client emails her team drafts and flag those that need her sign-off before they are sent. Her prompt gives the full background: an enterprise client, a second two-week delay to a software integration, and the professional but apologetic tone the account calls for. Its only instruction on flagging is "flag anything that looks risky." Claude flags about 20 of the 30 each week, most of them for informal greetings or long sentences, and her team has begun to skip the flags, including the few on emails that promise a delivery date.

What change to the prompt will most improve the result?

A. Add more background on the client, the integration and the history of the two delays.
B. Add an instruction to be conservative and to flag an email only when highly confident.
C. Ask Claude to rate each email's risk from 1 to 10 and to list those rated 8 or above.
D. State what warrants a flag, such as a promised date, and what to skip, such as greetings.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. The prompt already has the background a drafting task would need; what it lacks is a definition of "risky", so Claude decides for itself and flags style. The exam guide's fix for false positives is explicit criteria that say which issues to report and which to skip, which is Option D; it also notes that a high false-positive rate erodes trust in the accurate findings, as the skipped delivery-date flags show. Option A is the remedy when output is generic for want of context, but more background does not say what to flag. Option B sets a general bar, and instructions such as "be conservative" or "only report high-confidence findings" do not improve precision the way specific categories do. Option C filters on a score that Claude assigns itself, which is confidence-based filtering with the criteria missing: a greeting that Claude considers risky simply scores high. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.1 References: • Prompting best practices: Be clear and direct (Claude API docs) • Code Review: What you can tune (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front:
A marketing manager used Research to produce a 20-page competitive brief in which the claims carry citations to their sources. For a leadership meeting in three days, she asked Claude in a separate chat to compress the brief into a two-page summary. The summary reads well, but the compression merged and reworded claims, and none of its statements carries a source. Leadership wants to be able to trace any statement in the two-page version back to where it came from.

What is the most reliable way to meet that requirement?

A. Redo the compression, telling Claude to keep beside each statement the citations of the claims behind it.
B. Append the complete list of the brief's sources to the two-page summary as a closing references section.
C. Spot-check the citations in the 20-page brief herself, and circulate the two-page summary as it stands.
D. Ask Claude to search the web for a page that supports each statement, and attach those pages as its sources.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Attribution is lost at summarization steps when findings are compressed without their claim-source mappings, which is what happened between the cited brief and the two-page version. The reliable remedy is to carry the mapping through that step: redo the compression so that each statement keeps the citations of the brief claims behind it and a reader can open the source for any statement. That is Option A. Option B restores the sources but not the mapping, so nobody can tell which of dozens of references supports a given sentence. Option C checks the brief, which is sound practice when citations are attached, but it leaves the summary's merged and reworded statements untraceable for its readers. Option D reconstructs provenance after the fact: a page found by a new search is not necessarily where a statement came from, and it may only appear to support it. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.6 References: • Reduce hallucinations: Basic hallucination minimization strategies (Claude API docs) • Use research on Claude (Claude Help Center) • Claude is providing incorrect or misleading responses. What's going on? (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front:
Evidence reviews for a public-health agency are produced by a multi-agent research system. Its search subagents return structured findings (claim, source, excerpt, publication date and study design), and a synthesis subagent turns them into a narrative. For a review of school-meal programs, six randomized trials agree that attendance improves slightly, while two large observational studies published in the same year reach opposite conclusions about the effect on test scores. The narrative folds all of this into one confident paragraph, and the agency's reviewers cannot tell which statements are settled and which are disputed.

Which change to the synthesis subagent's instructions best addresses this?

A. Require it to report the findings on which the sources agree and to leave the disputed ones out of the review.
B. Require it to attach a confidence percentage to each statement and to order the statements by that figure.
C. Require it to separate well-established from contested findings and to keep each source's wording and method.
D. Require it to adopt the conclusion of the larger study wherever two sources differ and to cite that study.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. The exam guide asks for synthesis output with explicit sections that distinguish well-established findings from contested ones, preserving each source's own characterization and methodological context, and for conflicts to be annotated with attribution rather than settled by picking a side. The six trials that agree and the two same-year studies that disagree are those two categories, so Option C shows the agency what is settled, what is disputed, and what kind of study stands behind each position. Option A hides the dispute, although an open question about test scores is itself something the agency needs to know. Option B adds a figure the synthesis subagent assigns itself; it does not show who disagrees or why, and self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated. Option D resolves the conflict arbitrarily, because a larger sample does not settle a disagreement between credible studies. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.6 References: • Prompting best practices: Research and information gathering (Claude API docs) • Subagents in the SDK: Benefits of using subagents (Claude Code docs)
